title.narrative: Internationella Kvinnoförbundet för Fred och Frihet - Regionalt MENA-projekt
Women's International League for Peace and Freedom (WILPF) MENA Project

description.narrative: Det övergripande målet för projektet är att bidra till att stödja lokala kvinnoledda organisationer och feministiska rörelser för fred i MENA-regionen så att de kan utveckla sina egna agendor, narrativ och perspektiv och kräva utrymme i beslutsfattande på lokal, nationell och internationell nivå, vilket sedermera förväntas bidra till en inkluderande, intersektionell och inflytelserik fredsrörelse.

The objective of the programme is to support local women-led organizations and feminist peace movements in the MENA region to develop their own agendas, narratives and perspectives and to claim spaces within decision-making at the local, national and international levels, to contribute to an inclusive, intersectional and powerful peace movement.

description.narrative:
The WILPF narrative report for 2024 establishes that there was a focus on establishing the relationship between WILPF and the new partners, and between the partners themselves. It gave the partners tools and strategies to apply to advancing in their own specific agendas the partners needs assessment were initiated multiple individual and collective conversations, dialogues and check ins were organised and partners were taught about WILPF MENA teams feminist approach in relationship building and approaching solidarity across the movement.
Results per output are presented below: Output 1: Feminist grassroot organisations and womenled initiatives are better resourced to focus on advancing their own feminist peace agendas
Flexible funding enabled WILPF to support 11 feminist organisations in six countries (Lebanon, Palestine, Jordan, Iraq, Morocco, Tunisia) to cover main operation costs, retain staff, and continue operating despite conflict, occupation, and authoritarian crackdowns. The organisations' work spanned four key areas: documentation as resistance, safe spaces and collective healing, advocacy and policy influence and survival, adaptation and sustainability. In Lebanon, partners were able to maintain the SRHR hotlines and support networks even under bombardments. A thematic case study was conducted to highlight how partners in Lebanon mobilised during the war to meet urgent needs while advancing feminist peace. It featured three stories of change together with the report to showcase examples and details on partner's advancement and capabilities. Stories from partners in Lebanon show how they navigated active conflict by adapting quickly to urgent needs. For example, the Knowledge Workshop shifted from its usual focus on feminist and environmental justice to immediate crisis response, enabled by its flexible funding and community rooted approach. These cases, according to WILPF, highlight the vital role such organisations play in both immediate crisis management and longterm community resilience, showing that longterm adaptability is a key to achieving lasting community empowerment and justice. Partner organisations have created archives and feminist narratives that safeguarded marginalised stories and documented abuse, including against Palestinian women with disabilities. Feminist clubs, craft circles and other collective learning communities gave women and marginalised groups the opportunity to get political education, a chance to recover and a sense of community. Grassroot research was transformed into policy demands and advocacy, such as the strengthened protection for migrant workers. The partner organisation in Tunisia, through the flexible funding provided by WILPF, has strengthened protection mechanisms and expanded support services for women and girls survivors of genderbased violence. The organisation launched a dedicated support cell that has provided direct assistance to women and girls. Services include: social support legal assistance, including free judicial support and coverage of legal fees for survivors of domestic violence psycho-social support and active listening access to shelters. The organisation has also introduced a mobile support unit operating across Tunis, including on weekends when most GBV services are unavailable but cases of violence are most prevalent. This initiative ensures that survivors can access immediate assistance during critical moments, even when other support systems are closed. The flexible funding model has enabled partners to prioritise adaptation and longterm movement building. Partners' budget allocations differed based on their priorities and agendas but three main priorities could be identified: core costs, capacity building, and knowledge production.
Output 2: Feminist grassroot organisations and womenled initiatives are technically supported to participate in and influence feminist peace. Through the project's Technical Support Plan, partner organisations have received training in WILPF's finance and procurement induction workshop. This is expected to lead to improved reporting capabilities and increased financial transparency among partners. Partner organisations were invited to individual Partners Needs Assessment (PNA), which helped the organisations complete the financial reports and address technical difficulties, building both administrative capacity and confidence. These individual assessments were conducted with all partners during the summer of 2024 and provided a deeper understanding of their collective needs, priorities, and challenges. The PNAs also showed a strong trend towards partners actively seeking regional and international collaborations. Insights from the assessments made it possible to give tailored support interventions and create a common basis for continued networking and solidarity in the region. In 2025, TSP will include learning sessions on decolonial feminism, resistance to militarisation, alternative financing, and strategies against digital violence against women. Partner organisations are involved in co-designing these activities.
Output 3: Feminist grassroot organisations and womenled initiatives have enhanced networking and movement building opportunities facilitated by WILPF The inception meeting in November 2024 brought together all partner organisations and the WILPF team. This meeting was intended to provide a space for building trust and relationships ahead of the regional gathering in Nairobi. The partners came together in an inclusive, partnered regional gathering in Nairobi. The gathering enabled joint analysis of structural oppression, such as colonialism, capitalism and militarism, and the development of strategies for transnational feminist solidarity. The gathering had four key discussions: global politics, militarization and capitalism, decreasing trust in multilateral spaces, NGOisation and funding, and building transnational feminist solidarity. The gathering further prioritised the development of knowledge and documentation. Together with partners, WILPF has produced podcasts, interviews, and informal storytelling sessions that centered feminist narratives and served as a tool for awareness raising. WILPF produced four episodes of the Political Is Personal Podcast series exploring topics such as backlash and feminist resistance in MENA, the impact of conflicts on economies through a feminist lens, the feminist movement in Sudan, and feminist leadership in times of crisis and disaster.
Output 4: Resourcing procedures at WILPF are enhanced for the feminist movement
The WILPF report states that the organisation has strengthened team integration and collaboration. The restructuring of the MENA team has enabled a more cohesive way of working, with staff working across projects and functions, reducing silos and strengthening internal capacity for crisis response. In terms of resourcing, WILPF chose to remove external consultants form the process and instead rely on internal staff to lead the enhancement of resourcing procedures. This decision was made to ensure full ownership and collective responsibility over the process and outcomes. One of the improvements was a modified partner selection approach designed to support more grassroots and radical feminist groups, particularly those working with niche, underserved and marginalised groups.
